# Prerequisites {#sec-prerequisites} ## Installing Julia {#sec-installing} Use **`juliaup`**, the official version manager. Do not install Julia through a system package manager (`apt`, `brew`), which tends to ship outdated versions. ::: {.panel-tabset} ## macOS and Linux ```bash curl -fsSL https://install.julialang.org | sh ``` ## Windows ```powershell winget install julia -s msstore ``` ::: Afterwards, `juliaup update` upgrades and `juliaup status` lists installed versions. ## Project environments {#sec-environments} This is the most important concept in the chapter, and the one that differs most from common practice in R. In R, `install.packages()` installs into a global library shared by all your projects. In Julia, each project has its own environment, described by two files: - **`Project.toml`** — the direct dependencies you declared. - **`Manifest.toml`** — the full resolved dependency tree, with exact versions of everything. Together they make an analysis reproducible by construction: anyone who clones your repository and runs `Pkg.instantiate()` gets exactly your versions. ::: {.r-equivalent} **In R** `Project.toml` + `Manifest.toml` play the role of `renv.lock`, but they are part of the language rather than an add-on package. Activating an environment is the default operation, not the exception. ::: ::: {#env-status .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Pkg Pkg.status() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: ## This book's environment {#sec-book-environment} ::: {#versioninfo .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} versioninfo() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Julia Version 1.12.6 Commit 15346901f00 (2026-04-09 19:20 UTC) Build Info: Official https://julialang.org release Platform Info: OS: macOS (arm64-apple-darwin24.0.0) CPU: 10 × Apple M5 WORD_SIZE: 64 LLVM: libLLVM-18.1.7 (ORCJIT, apple-m1) GC: Built with stock GC Threads: 1 default, 1 interactive, 1 GC (on 4 virtual cores) Environment: JULIA_LOAD_PATH = @:@stdlib ``` ::: ::: To reproduce the book: ```bash git clone cd EcologicalAnalysesInJulia julia --project=. -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.instantiate()' ``` ## Editor {#sec-editor} **VS Code** with the official Julia extension is the standard recommendation: it offers an integrated REPL, a variable browser, a plot pane, a debugger and line-by-line evaluation — the functional equivalent of RStudio. If you prefer a fully open-source build, [VSCodium](https://vscodium.com) is VS Code compiled from the same MIT-licensed source without Microsoft's telemetry, and installs the same Julia extension from the [Open VSX](https://open-vsx.org) registry. Everything below applies to both. Alternatives: **Pluto.jl** (reactive notebooks, excellent for teaching) and any editor with LSP support through `LanguageServer.jl`. ### Setting up VS Code {#sec-vscode-setup} 1. **Install VS Code** from (or VSCodium). 2. **Install the Julia extension.** Open the Extensions panel (`Ctrl+Shift+X`; `Cmd+Shift+X` on macOS), search for *Julia* and install the extension published by *julialang*. It finds the Julia installed by `juliaup` on its own; if it does not, point the `julia.executablePath` setting at it. 3. **Open a folder, not a file.** Use *File → Open Folder…* and choose your project folder — for this book, the cloned `EcologicalAnalysesInJulia` folder. The folder determines both the working directory and the environment. 4. **Check the environment.** The status bar at the bottom should read `Julia env: EcologicalAnalysesInJulia`. When the folder contains both a `Project.toml` and a `Manifest.toml`, the extension activates it automatically; otherwise, click the status bar entry and choose the folder. 5. **Start the REPL.** Open the Command Palette (`Ctrl+Shift+P`; `Cmd+Shift+P` on macOS) and run *Julia: Start REPL*, or press `Alt+J` then `Alt+O`. The REPL starts in the folder root, with the active environment already loaded. ::: {.r-equivalent} **In R** Opening a folder in VS Code plays the role of opening an `.Rproj` in RStudio: it sets the working directory. Unlike RStudio, it also selects the package environment (@sec-environments), so the right package versions come along automatically. ::: The shortcuts you will use constantly: | Shortcut | Action | |---|---| | `Shift+Enter` | run the current line or selection, then move to the next | | `Ctrl+Enter` | run the current line or selection, staying put | | `Alt+Enter` | run the current cell (a block delimited by `##` lines) | | `Alt+J`, `Alt+R` | restart the REPL | | `Ctrl+C` in the REPL | interrupt a running computation | On macOS, `Alt` is the Option key; `Ctrl` stays `Ctrl`. Shortcuts and menu names were checked against version 1.249 of the Julia extension in September 2026. ### A first script {#sec-first-script} With the book folder open and the REPL running, create a file called `first-steps.jl` in the folder root (*File → New File*, or `Alt+J` then `Alt+N`) and paste: ```julia ## Load packages using CSV, DataFrames, CairoMakie ## Where am I? pwd() # the folder you opened readdir("data") # files inside data/ ## Read the example data ponds = CSV.read(joinpath("data", "ponds.csv"), DataFrame) first(ponds, 5) describe(ponds) ## Plot richness against pond area fig = Figure() ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "Pond area (m²)", ylabel = "Species richness", xscale = log10) scatter!(ax, ponds.area_m2, ponds.richness) fig ``` Put the cursor on the first cell and press `Alt+Enter` to run it, then keep going cell by cell (`Alt+Shift+Enter` runs the cell and jumps to the next one). A few things to notice: - **Loading packages is slow the first time** in each session — that is the compilation latency discussed in @sec-latency. Later cells run immediately. - **Paths are relative to the folder you opened.** `pwd()` confirms it, which is why `joinpath("data", "ponds.csv")` works without typing the full path. `joinpath` inserts the right separator on every operating system. - **`describe` is your first data check.** It shows that `canopy` has 7 missing values and that `area_m2` is strongly right-skewed (median around 149 m², maximum near 2000 m²) — which is why the plot uses a log scale. **Inspecting the environment.** Click the Julia icon in the Activity Bar (the left-hand strip). The **Workspace** panel lists every variable in the session — `ponds`, `fig`, `ax` — with its type and size; expand an entry to look inside. For a data frame, hover over its name and click the *Open in VS Code* icon, or run `vscodedisplay(ponds)` in the REPL, to open it in a spreadsheet-like grid — the equivalent of RStudio's `View()`. **Plots.** Evaluating `fig` opens the figure in the **plot pane**, a VS Code tab. The **Plot Navigator** panel, below the Workspace, keeps the history of the session's plots; with the plot pane focused, the arrow keys move through it. To save a figure to disk, use `save("richness-area.png", fig)`. ## Quarto {#sec-quarto} This book is written in [Quarto](https://quarto.org), the direct successor to `bookdown`. Since version 1.5, Quarto executes Julia blocks natively, without going through Jupyter. ````markdown ```{{julia}} #| label: example 1 + 1 ``` ```` ## Exercises {.unnumbered} 1. Create a new environment with `] activate .` in an empty folder and add `DataFrames`. Inspect the generated `Project.toml`. 2. Delete `Manifest.toml` and run `Pkg.resolve()`. What changes? 3. Run `first-steps.jl` (@sec-first-script) cell by cell. In the Workspace panel, which types did `CSV.jl` assign to the `region` and `canopy` columns, and why is the type of `canopy` different from that of `area_m2`?
